Still clad in his bright yellow pressure suit, a visibly frustrated Fournier waved away cameras after his balloon's abrupt departure. It drifted back to the ground about 40 km away. Fournier says he spent nearly 12.7 million euros ($20 million) on his quest, a risky endeavor that French authorities refused to allow him to attempt over France. The ambitious mission came to an abrupt halt when an electrical charge caused the cable connecting the balloon to Fournier's gondola to snap. Without the tether holding it in place, the massive balloon drifted away into the sky, leaving Fournier grounded and his historic jump unrealized.

French parachutist Michel Fournier watched his dreams of stratospheric glory literally drift away into the Saskatchewan sky on Saturday, as his second attempt at a record-breaking skydive from the edge of space ended in failure before it truly began.

The 64-year-old adventurer, who has spent nearly two decades and over $20 million pursuing his ambition to break four world records simultaneously—including the highest parachute jump and longest free fall in history—had assembled his team near Saskatoon for what was meant to be the culmination of years of preparation. The plan called for a massive helium balloon to lift a specially designed gondola, with Fournier inside a pressurized capsule, to an altitude of roughly 40 kilometers above the Earth's surface, from which point he would leap into the thin stratospheric air and free-fall for several minutes before his parachute deployed.

But the mission unraveled in dramatic fashion during the launch sequence. As ground crews worked to connect Fournier's capsule to the balloon's tethering cable, a sudden electrical charge—likely generated by static buildup or atmospheric conditions—severed the critical connection. Freed from its mooring before the capsule could be properly attached, the enormous balloon began to drift away over the Canadian prairie, rising uselessly into the sky without its intended passenger.

Ground teams could only watch as months of meticulous planning and a fortune in specialized equipment floated out of reach. The balloon, along with the gondola, was left to soar unmanned, eventually coming down at an undetermined location, marking yet another costly setback in Fournier's long quest.

Aviation and aerospace experts who reviewed the incident described it as a "freak accident"—an unfortunate confluence of atmospheric electricity and mechanical timing that no amount of preparation could have fully anticipated. Static electrical discharges, while not unheard of during high-altitude balloon operations, are notoriously difficult to predict, and the severed cable represented a rare failure point in an otherwise well-tested system.

For Fournier, however, the setback was merely the latest chapter in a saga marked by repeated delays and disappointments. His quest to claim the records for highest ascent, highest parachute jump, longest free fall, and fastest free-fall speed has spanned years, weathering technical failures, funding challenges, and now this bizarre mechanical catastrophe. Despite the financial and emotional toll of Saturday's failure, the veteran skydiver remained defiant in his determination to complete the jump.

Speaking to reporters in the aftermath of the failed launch, Fournier vowed that this would not be the end of his ambitions. He announced plans to make another attempt in August, giving his team several weeks to recover the lost equipment, address the electrical vulnerability that doomed this launch, and prepare for what he hopes will finally be his moment of triumph.

The Frenchman's persistence in the face of repeated setbacks has become almost as much a part of his story as the record attempt itself. Having invested both his personal fortune and decades of his life into this singular goal, Fournier appears unwilling to let a freak electrical mishap—however costly—stand between him and his place in the history books.

Whether August will finally bring the successful launch that has eluded him for so long remains to be seen, but for now, Fournier and his team return to the drawing board, determined to overcome yet another obstacle in their extraordinary journey to the edge of space.

The balloon, constructed from ultra-thin polyethylene film designed to expand to nearly the size of a football stadium at peak altitude, is particularly vulnerable to microtears during inflation. Engineers identified a compromised seam near the apex that they believe developed during the unfurling process, when strong ground-level winds caused the material to twist against support lines.

"At altitudes where we're operating, even a pinhole leak becomes catastrophic," said the mission's technical director. "We simply couldn't guarantee the integrity of the envelope for a flight of this duration."

**The Gondola:** Compounding the balloon issue, engineers also flagged an anomaly in the gondola's life-support pressurization system during final systems checks. A faulty valve regulator failed to maintain consistent cabin pressure readings, raising concerns about the capsule's ability to protect the pilot during the multi-hour ascent through the stratosphere, where external temperatures can plummet to -70°F (-57°C) and atmospheric pressure drops to near-vacuum conditions.

Mission director [Name] emphasized that the decision to scrub the launch, while disappointing, was made with pilot safety as the paramount concern.

"We build in redundancies specifically so that when something like this happens, we catch it on the ground rather than at 100,000 feet," the director stated. The pilot, visibly disappointed but supportive of the decision, addressed the crowd briefly: "This is the nature of pushing boundaries. I trust this team completely, and I'll be ready the moment they tell me we're good to go."

The current world record for highest freefall jump stands at 128,100 feet, set in 2014. Today's team had hoped to surpass that mark by several thousand feet, potentially reclaiming a record that has changed hands multiple times over the past decade.

# Balloon Experiment Grounded After Freak Bird Strike Sends Payload Crashing Into County Fairground

**MILLBROOK, Ohio (CNN)** — What was supposed to be a routine high-altitude test of a new parachute deployment system ended in chaos Tuesday afternoon when a flock of geese collided with a research balloon at approximately 62,000 feet, sending the experimental payload plummeting into an empty carnival tent at the Millbrook County Fairgrounds below.

No injuries were reported, though officials say the incident could have been catastrophic had the fair, which opens this weekend, already been in full swing.

## A Test Years in the Making

The project, led by aerospace engineering firm Stratosphere Dynamics, aimed to test a new autonomous parachute system designed for near-space equipment recovery. The balloon, carrying a 340-pound dummy payload rigged with sensors and cameras, launched from a nearby field just after 9 a.m.

"We had run the numbers a hundred times over," said lead engineer Dana Whitfield, visibly shaken during a press briefing hours after the incident. "Weather models, wind shear, ascent rate — everything checked out. Nobody accounts for a migrating flock of Canada geese at 60,000 feet. Honestly, I'm not sure they should even be flying that high."

Preliminary telemetry data suggests at least two birds struck the balloon's envelope within seconds of each other, causing a rapid loss of lift on one side. The imbalance triggered an uncontrolled descent, and while the parachute system did partially deploy, it failed to fully stabilize the payload before impact.

"It's the kind of freak accident you plan for in theory but never actually expect," Whitfield added. "You write it into the risk assessment as a footnote, not a headline."

## Mayor: "Thank God It Missed the Midway"

Millbrook Mayor Carol Jennings arrived at the fairgrounds shortly after the payload came down, inspecting the crumpled tent and scattered debris field firsthand.

"I've been mayor of this town for eleven years, and I can honestly say I never thought I'd be looking at a piece of NASA-adjacent equipment sitting in the middle of our funnel cake stand," Jennings told reporters. "We are incredibly fortunate this happened on a Tuesday morning and not this weekend, when there would've been thousands of people here."

Jennings said the town had approved the balloon launch months in advance and had been assured the flight path posed no risk to the fairgrounds.

"They told us the trajectory kept it miles away," she said. "But I guess nobody asks the geese for their flight plan."

The mayor said she's requested a full incident report from Stratosphere Dynamics before granting any future permits for aerial testing near town property.

## Technical Team Reviewing Everything

Stratosphere Dynamics has grounded all further test flights pending an internal review. Whitfield said the team is particularly interested in reexamining the balloon's structural resilience to impacts and whether additional sensors could detect wildlife at extreme altitudes in the future.

"We build for turbulence, we build for equipment failure, we even build for lightning strikes," she said. "Bird strikes at 62,000 feet — that's not something in our standard playbook. It will be now."

The company confirmed the payload itself, though damaged, yielded valuable data before the collision, and portions of the test may be considered a partial success despite the dramatic ending.

## No Injuries, But Fair Organizers Rattled

Fairground staff, who were on-site conducting final safety inspections ahead of the weekend's opening, described hearing a loud whistling sound followed by a crash.

"We thought maybe it was fireworks testing gone wrong," said fairground operations manager Pete Alvarez. "Then we walked over and there's this — thing — sitting in a pile of collapsed tent poles. Took us a solid minute to figure out what we were even looking at."

Alvarez said the tent will need to be replaced before the fair opens Friday, but organizers don't expect the incident to delay the event.

As for the geese, wildlife experts say the birds were likely unharmed, or at most stunned briefly, given similar high-altitude bird strikes documented in aviation history — though rarely at such an extreme altitude.

"It really is one in a million," Whitfield said. "Just our luck it happened on test day."

*CNN has reached out to the FAA for comment on airspace protocols involving high-altitude balloon testing near populated areas.*
